blocks.text:
High-level design decides which services and data stores exist. Low-level design (LLD) decides how the code inside one service is shaped: which classes exist, what each one is responsible for, how they depend on one another, and where the program is expected to change. A design that passes every test today but forces edits in five classes for each new requirement is a poor design, and LLD interviews and code reviews measure exactly that property.

This chapter states the principles used throughout the rest of the part. Each principle is shown with a violation and a repair, written in Java 21 and executed. The complete listing for the chapter is a single file, `Principles.java`; the output of the whole program is shown at the end of the chapter.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Encapsulation and abstraction

**Encapsulation** keeps the state of an object private and exposes behaviour that preserves the invariants of that state. **Abstraction** exposes what an object does and hides how. The two are related but distinct: encapsulation protects data, abstraction hides detail.

blocks.title: Violation: public mutable state
Repair: private state, behaviour enforces the invariant

blocks.text:
The repaired `Account` cannot reach a negative balance through any public method. The invariant is stated and enforced in one place, so a reader needs to inspect only that class to trust it.

#### Inheritance versus composition

Inheritance models an is-a relationship and couples the subclass to every public and protected member of its parent, including members added in later versions. Composition models has-a: the class holds a collaborator and forwards only the calls it chooses to expose. The default choice is composition; inheritance is appropriate when the subclass is genuinely substitutable for the parent in every context (see the Liskov principle below) and the parent was designed for extension.

Repair: Stack2 wraps a Deque and exposes three methods

#### Polymorphism

Polymorphism lets a caller depend on an interface while the concrete behaviour is selected at run time by the receiver. It is the mechanism behind every pattern in the next chapter: the caller invokes `strategy.price(base)` and the object decides what that means. In Java, dynamic dispatch on interface and virtual methods provides it; the cost is one indirect call, which the JIT compiler usually removes for monomorphic call sites.

### SOLID with a violation and a repair for each principle

#### S: single responsibility

A class should have one reason to change. `InvoiceBad` below changes when the tax rate changes, when the output format changes and when the storage changes: three reasons. The repair separates calculation (`Invoice`), presentation (`InvoiceRenderer`) and persistence (`InvoiceStore`).

blocks.title: Violation: calculation, formatting and storage in one class
Repair: one responsibility per type

blocks.text:
#### O: open for extension, closed for modification

New behaviour should be added by writing new code, not by editing tested code. The `switch` in `discountBad` must be edited for every new customer category, and each edit risks the existing branches. With a `DiscountPolicy` interface, a new policy is a new class.

blocks.title: Violation: a switch that grows with every variant
Repair: a new discount is a new implementation

blocks.text:
A `switch` is not wrong in itself. Over a closed set that never grows, for example the four suits of a card deck, a `switch` over an enum or a sealed type is clearer than polymorphism. The principle applies where variants are expected to arrive.

#### L: Liskov substitution

Code written against a base type must keep working when a subtype is supplied. A `Square` that overrides `setWidth` to also change the height breaks the contract of `Rect`, because a caller that sets width 5 and height 4 expects an area of 20.

blocks.title: Violation: Square narrows the postcondition of Rect
Repair: immutable siblings under a sealed interface

blocks.text: The repair removes the false is-a relationship. Mutability was what made the relationship unsound; as immutable values, `Rectangle` and `Sq` share only the operation `area()`.

#### I: interface segregation

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. A `MultiFunctionDevice` interface forces a basic printer to implement `scan` and `fax` with empty or exception-throwing bodies. Small role interfaces (`Printer`, `Scanner2`) let each class implement exactly what it supports.

blocks.title: Violation: one fat interface
Repair: role interfaces

#### D: dependency inversion

High-level policy should depend on abstractions, and low-level details should depend on the same abstractions. `OrderServiceBad` constructs `MySqlOrderRepo` itself, so the service cannot be tested without a database and cannot change its store without being edited. Passing an `OrderRepository` through the constructor inverts the dependency; this is exactly what constructor injection in Spring provides.

Repair: depend on an interface, inject the implementation

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Anemic domain model with logic scattered in services

**Scenario.** A billing service keeps `Invoice` as a bag of getters and setters, and five service classes each recompute totals.

**Symptoms.** A tax change requires edits in five places; two of them are missed and the totals differ between the web screen and the exported PDF.

**Diagnosis.** Search for the formula shows duplicates; `Invoice` has no behaviour.

**Root cause.** The rule has no single owner (violation of DRY and of encapsulation).

**Fix.** Move the calculation into `Invoice.total()` and make the fields private.

**Prevention.** Review rule: logic that reads only one object's fields belongs on that object.

#### Inheritance used for code reuse

**Scenario.** `ReportExporter extends ArrayList<Row>` to reuse list operations.

**Symptoms.** A library upgrade adds a default method on `List`; callers start invoking it on exporters with undefined results. Serialisation of the subclass also leaks the list internals.

**Diagnosis.** `ReportExporter` is not a list in any domain sense; the dependency was introduced only for convenience.

**Root cause.** Inheritance chosen over composition.

**Fix.** Hold a `List<Row>` field and expose `add(Row)` and `export()`.

**Prevention.** Ask whether the subclass can be used wherever the parent is used. If not, use composition.

#### Tests that need a database

**Scenario.** Unit tests of `OrderService` take four minutes because the service creates a real repository.

**Symptoms.** Tests fail when the shared test database is unavailable; developers skip them.

**Diagnosis.** The constructor calls `new MySqlOrderRepo()`.

**Root cause.** Violation of dependency inversion.

**Fix.** Introduce `OrderRepository`, inject it, and use `InMemoryOrderRepo` in unit tests.

**Prevention.** Allow `new` of collaborators only in composition roots (the application configuration or `main`).

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why is composition preferred over inheritance?** A. Inheritance binds a subclass to the full parent API and to its implementation details at compile time; composition binds only to the methods called, allows the collaborator to be replaced at run time, and avoids fragile base-class changes.
- **Q. Give a Liskov violation that is not Rectangle and Square.** A. A `ReadOnlyList` subclass of `List` whose `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`: callers written against `List` fail. Java's `List.of` has this shape, which is why APIs should accept `Collection` or `Iterable` when they only read.
- **Q. How do open/closed and a** `switch` **relate?** A. A `switch` on a type code is a signal that each new type edits the method. Polymorphism or a sealed hierarchy with pattern matching moves the variation to new types. A closed set of variants may keep the `switch`.
- **Q. What is the difference between dependency inversion and dependency injection?** A. Inversion is the design rule: depend on abstractions. Injection is a technique for supplying the implementation from outside. Spring provides injection; the rule is still the developer's responsibility.
- **Q. When does applying SOLID hurt?** A. When it creates interfaces with one implementation and no foreseeable second one. The extra indirection costs readability without buying flexibility; apply a principle where change is expected.
- **Q. What is cohesion and how is it recognised?** A. Cohesion measures how strongly the members of a class relate. A class whose methods use disjoint subsets of its fields is a candidate for splitting.

Encapsulate invariants: private state, behaviour that rejects invalid transitions.

- Prefer composition; inherit only when substitutability holds in every context.
- SRP counts reasons to change, OCP removes edits from tested code, LSP keeps subtypes honest, ISP shrinks interfaces, DIP points dependencies at abstractions.
- DRY, KISS and YAGNI are balancing forces; abstract on the third occurrence, not the first.
- Run the checks mentally: can the class be tested without infrastructure, and does a new requirement add a class or edit five?

A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem, stated at the level of classes and their collaboration. The value of a pattern in an interview is a shared vocabulary: saying "the elevator uses the State pattern and dispatch is a Strategy" conveys a structure in one sentence. The value in production is the same, plus the knowledge of where the pattern costs more than it returns.

Thirteen patterns that recur in machine-coding problems are covered here. Each entry gives the intent, the structure, Java code that was run, and a place where the pattern already exists in the JDK or in Spring. Two programs hold all the code: `Patterns1.java` (creational patterns, Strategy and Observer) and `Patterns2.java` (structural patterns, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility and Template Method).

#### Singleton

A singleton restricts a class to one instance. Three thread-safe forms are shown. The **enum** form is the shortest and is safe against serialisation and reflection attacks. The **initialisation-on-demand holder** is lazy because the nested class loads on first use, and class initialisation is guaranteed thread-safe by the JVM. **Double-checked locking** works only when the field is `volatile`; without it another thread may observe a partially constructed object.

blocks.title: Singleton: enum, holder and double-checked locking
Gotcha
blocks.text: A Spring singleton bean is one instance per application context, not one per JVM, and it is created by the container, not by a static method. Hand-written singletons hide dependencies, are hard to replace in tests and are shared mutable state across the whole process. Prefer a container-managed singleton and constructor injection; keep the hand-written form for genuinely process-wide resources such as a logger registry.

### Behavioural patterns, first group

#### Observer

A subject keeps a list of listeners and calls each when an event occurs. The publisher knows only the `OrderListener` interface. Notice `List.copyOf(listeners)`: iterating a snapshot lets a listener subscribe or unsubscribe during notification without a `ConcurrentModificationException`. Spring offers the same model with `ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent` and `@EventListener`; the JDK has `PropertyChangeListener` and the `java.util.concurrent.Flow` interfaces.

blocks.text:
### Structural patterns

#### Decorator

A decorator implements the interface it wraps and forwards calls, adding behaviour before or after. Decorators compose: `Caramel(Milk(Espresso))` costs 80 + 15 + 25. It is the alternative to a subclass explosion (`EspressoWithMilkAndCaramel`). `java.io` is the canonical case.

blocks.title: Decorator: stackable add-ons with the same interface

blocks.text:
#### Adapter

An adapter translates between an existing interface (the legacy bank takes paise as a `long`) and the one the client requires (`pay(int rupees)`). The client stays unaware of the legacy API, and the unit conversion is confined to one class.

blocks.title: Adapter: legacy API behind the expected interface

blocks.text:
#### Proxy

A proxy has the same interface as the real object and controls access: lazy loading, access control, caching or timing. The JDK dynamic proxy creates the stand-in at run time for interfaces; Spring AOP uses it (or CGLIB for classes) to implement `@Transactional`. A consequence worth knowing: a call from one method to another inside the same object bypasses the proxy, so the advice does not run.

blocks.title: Proxy: a timing proxy with java.lang.reflect.Proxy

blocks.text:
#### Facade

A facade offers a narrow entry point over several collaborating subsystems. `OrderFacade.placeOrder` hides the order of reservation, payment and shipping. It does not prevent direct access to the subsystems; it only provides the convenient path.

blocks.title: Facade: one call over three subsystems

blocks.text:
### Behavioural patterns, second group

#### Command

A command object bundles an action and the data needed to run it. Because it is an object it can be stored, queued, logged and reversed. `History` keeps executed commands on a stack, so `undo()` pops and reverses the last one. In the JDK, `Runnable` and `Callable` handed to an executor are commands.

blocks.title: Command: execute and undo

blocks.text:
#### State

The state pattern replaces a conditional on a status field with polymorphism: each state decides which event leads where. The door example uses an enum with an abstract method; larger machines (elevator, vending machine, order lifecycle) use one class per state so that each can hold its own logic. Unlisted transitions stay in the same state, or throw, and that policy should be explicit.

blocks.title: State: transitions owned by the state

blocks.text:
#### Chain of Responsibility

A request passes through a chain of handlers, each of which handles it or forwards it. The sender knows only the first handler, and the order of handlers can be changed by configuration. Servlet filters and the Spring Security filter chain follow this structure; in those chains every filter normally forwards, which is the variant used by the logger problem later in this part.

blocks.title: Chain of Responsibility: approval limits

blocks.text:
#### Template Method

An abstract class fixes the algorithm in a `final` method and leaves steps abstract (mandatory) or overridable (hooks). The framework controls the flow; the subclass supplies the steps. `JdbcTemplate` applies the same idea through callbacks instead of inheritance, which is the usual preference today because it composes better.

blocks.title: Template Method: fixed skeleton, variable steps

### Patterns overused and when not to apply them

Patterns solve variation. Where no variation exists, a pattern adds classes without adding flexibility.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Which pattern would model an elevator, and why? State for the car itself, because behaviour (accept a call, move, open the door) depends on the state and each transition belongs to a state object; Strategy for dispatch, because the policy for choosing a car is independent of the car and should be replaceable.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Memory leak through a registered listener

**Scenario.** A dashboard screen registers a listener with a long-lived event publisher each time it opens and never unregisters.

**Symptoms.** Heap grows by one screen object graph per open; old screens still react to events.

**Diagnosis.** A heap dump shows many screen instances retained by the publisher's `listeners` list.

**Root cause.** Observer registration without a removal path; the publisher holds a strong reference.

**Fix.** Unsubscribe in the screen's close method, or hold listeners through weak references, or scope the subscription to a lifetime object that removes it automatically.

**Prevention.** Every `subscribe` has a matching `unsubscribe`; return a handle from `subscribe` and use try-with-resources.

#### Double-checked locking without volatile

**Scenario.** A lazily created configuration object is accessed by request threads.

**Symptoms.** Rare `NullPointerException` on a field of the supposedly initialised instance, seen only under load and never in unit tests.

**Diagnosis.** The `instance` field is non-volatile.

**Root cause.** Without a happens-before edge, another thread may see the reference before the constructor writes are visible.

**Fix.** Declare the field `volatile`, or use the holder idiom or an enum.

**Prevention.** Default to the holder idiom or container-managed singletons; avoid double-checked locking.

#### Self-invocation bypasses the proxy

**Scenario.** A service method `save()` calls another method of the same class annotated `@Transactional`.

**Symptoms.** No transaction is opened for the inner call; a failure leaves partial data.

**Diagnosis.** Logs show no proxy frame between the two methods.

**Root cause.** Proxy-based AOP intercepts only calls that arrive through the proxy; `this.inner()` is a direct call.

**Fix.** Move the inner method to another bean, or restructure so that the annotated method is the entry point. **Prevention.** Know that the pattern is the mechanism: annotations on internal calls of a proxied bean have no effect.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Strategy versus State: both delegate to an interface.** A. In Strategy the client chooses the algorithm and it does not change by itself. In State the object changes its own delegate as events occur, and the states know each other.
- **Q. Decorator versus Proxy?** A. Same structure, different intent: a decorator adds responsibilities, a proxy controls access to the same responsibilities.
- **Q. Factory method versus Abstract Factory?** A. A factory method creates one product type; an abstract factory creates a family of related products that must be used together.
- **Q. Why is the enum singleton preferred?** A. The JVM guarantees one instance per constant, serialisation and reflection cannot create a second one, and no locking code is needed. Its limits are that it cannot extend a class and is always eagerly initialised on first access to the enum.
- **Q. Where is Template Method used in Spring?** A. `JdbcTemplate`, `RestTemplate` and `TransactionTemplate` fix the resource handling and error translation and leave the variable part to a callback.
- **Q. How is Chain of Responsibility different from a loop over handlers?** A. It is the same behaviour with the iteration encoded in the objects. The loop form is simpler when the list is static; the chain form lets a handler stop propagation or change what is passed on.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Patterns name solutions to variation: Strategy and Factory vary algorithm and creation, Observer and Command vary reaction and request, State varies behaviour by status.

- Decorator, Proxy and Adapter all wrap; ask whether the wrapper adds, controls or converts.
- Prefer enum or holder singletons, and container-managed singletons in Spring.
- Add a pattern only where a second variant is plausible; otherwise the pattern is cost.

A machine-coding or LLD round gives a short statement, for example "design a parking lot", and expects a compilable, extensible design in 45 to 90 minutes. The statement is deliberately incomplete. Candidates are judged on the method as much as the result: whether requirements were clarified, whether the classes model the domain, whether extension points are placed where change is likely, and whether concurrency was considered.

blocks.text:
### Worked example of the method

For "design a parking lot" the requirements step produces: vehicles are motorcycles, cars and trucks; spots have sizes; a vehicle takes the smallest free spot that fits; the lot issues a ticket at entry and charges at exit by hourly rate; several gates operate at the same time; payment and persistence are out of scope. The nouns are `Vehicle`, `ParkingSpot`, `Ticket`, `ParkingLot`; the verbs `park` and `exit` belong to `ParkingLot`; the two variations are spot selection and the fee rule, so those become strategies. Concurrency is the last step: two gates must never assign the same spot. The full solution appears as the first problem later in this part.

### Concurrency checklist

Concurrency is the step most often skipped and the one interviewers press on. The checklist below applies to every problem in this part.

1. Identify the shared mutable state: the maps, counters and status fields that two threads can touch.
2. For each, choose a protection: confinement to one thread, immutability, `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`, an atomic variable, or a concurrent collection.
3. Locate every check-then-act sequence (check availability, then take it); each must be atomic as a whole. A `ConcurrentHashMap` does not make two separate calls atomic.
4. Decide lock granularity: one lock for the object is simple; per-resource locks scale better but require a global acquisition order to avoid deadlock.
5. Keep slow work (I/O, calls to unknown code) outside locks.
6. Inject the clock and the random source so that time-dependent behaviour can be tested.
7. State what the design assumes: single JVM, in-memory state, and what would change if the state moved to a database.

### Hands-on: scoring your own design

Before moving to code, review the design against five questions. Each "no" is a defect to fix on paper, where it is cheaper than in code.

rows: Does each requirement map to a method on exactly one class?
Can a new variant (vehicle type, fee rule, notification channel) be added without editing existing classes?
Can every class be tested without threads, files or the network?
Is each invariant enforced in one place?
Which two operations may run concurrently, and which lock orders them?

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Over-designed solution that is not finished

**Scenario.** A candidate spends 40 minutes on abstract factories and plug-in interfaces for a parking lot and has no working `park` method.

**Symptoms.** The code does not compile at the end; the demo is missing.

**Diagnosis.** Time was spent on extension points before the base flow existed.

**Root cause.** YAGNI was ignored and the sequence of the method was inverted.

**Fix.** Implement the simplest end-to-end flow first, then extract the interface at each variation point named in the requirements.

**Prevention.** Time-box: 5 minutes requirements, 10 minutes entities and relations, 25 minutes code, 5 minutes extensions (assumed budget for a 45-minute round).

#### Requirements assumed instead of asked

**Scenario.** The candidate models a library with books only; the interviewer then asks about members with borrowing limits and fines.

**Symptoms.** The class model must be restructured late.

**Diagnosis.** No explicit list of use cases was agreed at the start.

**Root cause.** The first step was skipped.

**Fix.** Write the use cases on the board and have the interviewer confirm them.

**Prevention.** Ask about actors, scale, concurrency and persistence in every problem.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. How are entities distinguished from attributes?** A. A noun that has its own behaviour or lifecycle becomes a class; a noun that only describes another becomes a field or a value type (record).
- **Q. When should a method be a static utility?** A. Rarely: when it is a pure function of its arguments with no state and no variation, for example a parsing helper. Behaviour that varies belongs behind an interface.
- **Q. How much concurrency is expected in a machine-coding round?** A. At least the identification of the shared state and a correct choice for the critical check-then-act operation, stated aloud, even when the solution is single-threaded.
- **Q. What is the difference between a class diagram and a sequence diagram?** A. A class diagram describes what exists and how the types relate; a sequence diagram describes the order of calls in one scenario.
- **Q. Records, enums and sealed interfaces: when?** A. Records for immutable data carriers, enums for closed sets of constants with behaviour, sealed interfaces for closed variants that pattern matching can process exhaustively.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Where the race is.** The allocation loop reads the spot list and then claims a spot. Between those steps another gate may take it, which is why the claim is `tryPark` returning a boolean and the loop continues to the next candidate. The list itself is immutable after construction, so iteration needs no lock.

**Lock granularity.** One lock per spot allows gates to claim different spots in parallel. A single lot-wide lock would be simpler and would suffice for tens of requests per second; the finer lock matters only when allocation is a hot path.

**Cost.** `NearestTightFit` sorts all spots on every call, O(n log n). For thousands of spots keep free spots in a `TreeSet` ordered by (floor, size) per size class, or one `ConcurrentSkipListSet`, and poll from it.

**Extensions.** Add a new vehicle type: add an enum constant with a size. Electric charging spots: a spot attribute and a strategy that filters on it. Multiple lots: a `ParkingService` holding a map of lots. Persistence: replace the in-memory ticket map with a repository interface; the atomic claim then becomes a database update with a condition (`UPDATE` `spot SET vehicle = ? WHERE id = ? AND vehicle IS NULL`), as in the databases material.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Two vehicles assigned the same spot

**Scenario.** An earlier version checked `spot.isFree()` and then called `spot.assign(v)` in two statements.

**Symptoms.** Occasionally two tickets reference one spot; free-spot count becomes negative.

**Diagnosis.** A test with several threads and a small lot reproduces it; ticket spot ids contain duplicates.

**Root cause.** Check-then-act without atomicity.

**Fix.** A single `synchronized tryPark` that checks and sets under the same monitor.

**Prevention.** Name atomic operations as one method; run a multi-threaded test that asserts the count of successes equals the capacity.

#### Ticket reused at the exit

**Scenario.** A driver photographs a ticket and two exits process it.

**Symptoms.** Revenue is correct but the free-spot count increases twice and a second vehicle is assigned an occupied spot.

**Diagnosis.** Active tickets were read with `get` and removed later.

**Root cause.** Non-atomic read-then-remove.

**Fix.** `remove(ticketId)` as the first step; a null result means the ticket is unknown or already used.

**Prevention.** The operation that consumes a token must also invalidate it atomically.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why a Strategy for allocation instead of an** `if` **on vehicle type?** A. Allocation policy varies independently of the vehicle (site rules, pricing tiers). A strategy lets it change without editing `ParkingLot`.
- **Q. How would the lot support reservations?** A. Add a `RESERVED` spot state with an expiry, similar to the seat hold in the booking problem, and let the allocation strategy skip reserved spots.
- **Q. How is the free-spot count kept O(1)?** A. Maintain an `AtomicInteger` per size class updated in `tryPark` and `free`, or keep free spots in per-size queues; counting by scanning is O(n).
- **Q. How would this run across several servers?** A. The spot becomes a row; the claim becomes a conditional update or a distributed lock with a fencing token; the lot service is stateless.
- **Q. Why is time injected?** A. A test advances the clock to verify fees without sleeping, and the production clock can be replaced by a monotonic or synchronised source.

When the cache is full a `put` of a new key evicts one entry chosen by policy: least recently used (LRU) or least frequently used (LFU). The cache is shared by several threads. Out of scope: expiry by time, loading on a miss, statistics beyond a hit ratio, and distribution (see the caching material for cache-aside and distributed caches).

### Concurrency and extensions

**Why reads take the lock.** A `get` moves a node to the front. Any design that records recency on reads has writes on the read path. Production caches such as Caffeine avoid a lock on reads by recording accesses in a buffer and applying them in batches; that is an optimisation to mention, not to implement in an interview.

**Contention.** One lock serialises all operations. Striping the cache into N independent segments by `hash(key) % N` reduces contention at the cost of an approximate global policy (each segment evicts independently).

**Extensions.** Time-based expiry: store an expiry instant per node and check it on `get`. Loading: a `computeIfAbsent`-style method that holds a per-key lock to prevent a stampede. Eviction listener: call a callback with the victim. Memory bound: replace `capacity` with a weight function.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: LFU has a known weakness: an entry that was popular long ago keeps a high count and may never be evicted, so the cache fills with stale hot entries. Real implementations age the counts (decay) or combine recency and frequency, as TinyLFU does.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Unbounded growth from a plain HashMap used as cache

**Scenario.** A service caches product details in a `HashMap` with no limit.

**Symptoms.** Heap usage grows over days; garbage collection pauses lengthen; eventually `OutOfMemoryError`.

**Diagnosis.** A heap histogram shows the map and its values dominating the heap.

**Root cause.** No eviction policy and no maximum size.

**Fix.** Use a bounded cache (this chapter's LRU or a library cache) with a capacity derived from the memory budget.

**Prevention.** Every cache has a bound and an eviction policy; expose size and hit ratio as metrics.

#### Corrupted list under concurrent access

**Scenario.** An LRU built on `LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true)` is shared without synchronisation, on the assumption that reads are safe.

**Symptoms.** `ConcurrentModificationException`, infinite loops, or entries missing.

**Diagnosis.** A multi-threaded test fails; a thread dump shows threads spinning inside `LinkedHashMap`.

**Root cause.** With access order enabled `get` is a structural modification.

**Fix.** Guard every operation with one lock, or use a library cache.

**Prevention.** Treat reads as writes for any structure that tracks access.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why a doubly linked list and not a singly linked one?** A. Removing a node from the middle in O(1) requires its predecessor; the previous pointer provides it without a search.
- **Q. Why sentinels?** A. They remove the null checks for the first and last node, so `unlink` and `addFirst` are uniform.
- **Q. What is the complexity of the LFU described?** A. O(1) for `get` and `put`: map lookups, a `LinkedHashSet` removal and insertion, and an integer update for `minFreq`.
- **Q. How is it made faster under high concurrency?** A. Stripe into segments, or buffer recency updates and apply them asynchronously, accepting that recency is slightly stale.
- **Q. LRU or LFU for a product catalogue?** A. A stable popular set favours LFU; a workload with shifting popularity (news) favours LRU. Measure the hit ratio on a recorded trace; there is no universal answer.
- **Q. What happens when** `put` **is called for an existing key?** A. The value is replaced and the entry becomes most recent (LRU) or its frequency increases (LFU); no eviction occurs.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
LRU is a hash map plus a doubly linked list: O(1) lookup, O(1) reorder, eviction at `tail.prev`.

- LFU is a key-to-frequency map plus frequency buckets and `minFreq`; ties use insertion order.
- A cache that tracks access turns reads into writes, so reads need the lock.
- Bound every cache, and measure the hit ratio before choosing the policy.

Walk through the trace. Car 1 starts with a stop at floor 8. At tick 1 the call at floor 3 goes to car 0, which is idle and closer. At tick 2 the call at floor 6 (direction DOWN) goes to car 1; both cars are heading up, so both receive a penalty and car 1 wins on distance. Car 1 stops at 6 on its way to 8. This exposes a limitation of the simple version: the stop at 6 serves a DOWN request while the car is travelling up, so the passenger is picked up and carried in the wrong direction. Handling this properly requires stops to carry a direction (separate up and down sets), listed under extensions.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Thread safety.** Hall-call threads call `addStop` and the tick thread calls `step`; both are `synchronized` on the elevator, so the stop set is never modified during a decision. The controller picks a car by reading its floor and heading without the lock; a slightly stale read can choose a sub-optimal car but cannot corrupt state. A production system would serialise all requests through one event loop (a single-threaded executor), which removes most locking.

**Extensions.**

- Directional stops: keep `upStops` and `downStops`; a hall call joins the set of its direction, and the car serves the set that matches its heading.
- Capacity and overload: a `load` field and a state that refuses further stops when full.
- Maintenance mode: a new state that clears stops and rejects requests, added without editing the existing states.
- Dispatch by estimated time of arrival: a new strategy that sums remaining stops ahead of the call.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Starvation of a floor

**Scenario.** A policy that always serves the nearest stop is used.

**Symptoms.** A passenger on floor 1 waits a long time while floors near the car keep generating calls.

**Diagnosis.** Wait-time metrics show a long tail for floors far from the busiest zone.

**Root cause.** Nearest-first has no fairness bound.

**Fix.** Use a sweep policy (LOOK or SCAN): the car serves every stop in its direction, then reverses, so any stop is served within one sweep.

**Prevention.** Test with a trace that contains a persistent cluster of nearby requests and assert a maximum wait.

#### Car assigned by stale state

**Scenario.** Two hall calls arrive within the same tick and both choose the same idle car, leaving another car idle.

**Symptoms.** One car carries all calls; average wait increases.

**Diagnosis.** Dispatch logs show identical car ids for simultaneous calls. **Root cause.** The strategy reads `heading` while the previous assignment has not yet changed it; the new stop is added but the car is still IDLE.

**Fix.** Include the number of pending stops in the cost, or make assignment and cost update one atomic step in the controller.

**Prevention.** The cost function must see all assignments already made.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why State instead of an enum with a switch?** A. Each state has its own transition logic and may acquire its own data (door timer, maintenance reason). New states are new classes; the elevator is not edited.
- **Q. SCAN versus LOOK?** A. SCAN travels to the end of the shaft before reversing; LOOK reverses at the last requested stop and wastes less travel.
- **Q. How would several cars share load?** A. A dispatch strategy that estimates the time to serve a call for each car and picks the minimum, with penalties for cars heading away.
- **Q. How is a hall call distinguished from a destination button?** A. A hall call carries a direction and is assigned by the controller; a destination is a stop added to a known car.
- **Q. Where would an emergency stop fit?** A. As a state reachable from any state, with `step` doing nothing; the controller stops dispatching to the car.

- LOOK serves stops in the heading direction first, bounding the wait of every floor.
- A `TreeSet` makes "is there a stop above or below" a logarithmic query.
- Direction-aware stops and atomic cost updates are the main known extensions.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Thread safety.** All mutating and reading methods of `ExpenseManager` are `synchronized` on the manager. An expense touches several balances, so the update must be atomic as a whole; per-user locks would need an ordering to avoid deadlock for no real gain at this scale.

**Greedy is not optimal in general.** Finding the minimum number of transfers is NP-hard (it is equivalent to partitioning the balances into the maximum number of zero-sum subsets). The greedy method yields at most n-1 transfers and is correct in the sense that it settles every balance, which is the usual expectation. State this explicitly if asked about optimality.

**Extensions.** Groups: a `Group` entity with its own manager. Currencies: store `Money(amount, currency)` and convert at settlement. Audit: an append-only list of expenses from which balances can be recomputed (event sourcing). Persistence: expenses in a table, balances as a derived view, as in the databases material.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### A cent that disappears

**Scenario.** An equal split of Rs 100.00 among three users is computed with `double` and division.

**Symptoms.** Balances sum to 0.01 or -0.01 instead of zero; reconciliation reports small differences that accumulate.

**Diagnosis.** Summing all shares and comparing with the total shows a mismatch.

**Root cause.** Rounding each share independently loses or creates smallest units.

**Fix.** Integer minor units and an explicit remainder rule so that shares always add up to the total.

**Prevention.** Assert that the shares of every expense sum to its total; assert that all net balances sum to zero.

#### Partial update on failure

**Scenario.** An expense with an invalid percentage split throws after the payer's balance was already credited.

**Symptoms.** Balances no longer sum to zero.

**Diagnosis.** The invariant test fails after a rejected expense.

**Root cause.** State was changed before validation completed.

**Fix.** Compute all shares first (validation happens in `shares`), then apply updates; the code does this.

**Prevention.** Validate, then mutate; make the mutation step unable to fail.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why not** `double` **for money?** A. Binary fractions cannot represent most decimals; errors accumulate. Use integer minor units or `BigDecimal` with an explicit rounding mode.
- **Q. How does simplification work?** A. Compute net balance per user, put creditors and debtors in two max-heaps, repeatedly match the largest of each and transfer the smaller of the two amounts.
- **Q. Is the result minimal?** A. Not guaranteed; the exact minimum is NP-hard. The greedy result has at most n-1 transfers.
- **Q. How would a new split type, for example by shares, be added?** A. A new record implementing `Split` with its own validation and `shares`; no other class changes.
- **Q. How is idempotency handled if the client retries an expense?** A. Each expense carries a client-generated id; the manager ignores an id it has already applied.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Money is integer paise; every split must add up to the total, and every set of net balances must add up to zero.

- Split variants are a sealed interface, so new variants do not change the manager.
- Net balances drive settlement; the greedy matching yields at most n-1 transfers, not necessarily the minimum.
- Validate first, then mutate, under one lock.

### Requirements and use cases

A machine sells products from coded slots. The user inserts coins, selects a product, and receives the product and change. The user may cancel before selecting and receive a refund. The machine must reject operations that make no sense in its current state, for example a selection before any money is inserted.

rows: Whole-rupee coins of 10, 5, 2 and 1; change by greedy largest-first (optimal for this denomination set).
Quantity per product code; a sold-out product is rejected without consuming credit.
One user at a time; the public methods are `synchronized` to keep state changes atomic if a service layer calls from several threads.
Card payment, limited coin reserves in the machine, maintenance mode, and hardware faults.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Thread safety.** The three public methods are `synchronized`, so a transition and the credit update are atomic. Since the sale happens within `select`, no other thread can observe the machine in `DISPENSING` through the public API; the state exists for clarity and for future asynchronous hardware calls.

**Extensions.**

- Limited change: `ChangeMaker` consults a coin inventory and may fail; the machine then refunds in `HasMoneyState`.
- Out of service: a new state returned when a sensor fails; every operation throws or refunds.
- Different payment methods: a `PaymentMethod` strategy replaces `insertCoin`.
- Restocking: an admin interface separate from the user interface (interface segregation).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Greedy change-making is optimal only for canonical coin systems such as 10, 5, 2, 1. For arbitrary denominations a dynamic programming solution is required, which is the classic coin change problem from the DSA material.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Product dispensed but money not recorded

**Scenario.** The sale decrements inventory, then an exception occurs while computing change.

**Symptoms.** Stock decreases and credit remains; the next user receives the leftover credit.

**Diagnosis.** Inventory changed before all fallible steps completed.

**Root cause.** Mutations ordered before validation of the whole operation.

**Fix.** Compute change first, then take stock, then clear credit; failures before the take leave state unchanged.

**Prevention.** Order each operation: validate, compute, then mutate; test failure injection at each step.

#### Machine stuck in DISPENSING

**Scenario.** The dispense step throws and the state was already set to `DispensingState`.

**Symptoms.** Every later operation is rejected with "not allowed in state DISPENSING".

**Diagnosis.** The state name in the error shows the machine never returned to IDLE.

**Root cause.** The transition back is on the success path only.

**Fix.** Wrap the dispense in try/finally that restores a safe state and refunds on failure.

**Prevention.** A state that is entered must have a guaranteed exit.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Why State instead of boolean flags?** A. Flags such as `hasMoney` and `dispensing` multiply into invalid combinations; states make legal combinations explicit and give each its own code.
- **Q. How are illegal operations handled?** A. A default interface method throws; alternatives are to ignore the call or return a result object. Throwing is appropriate for programmer errors, a result for user mistakes.
- **Q. Where is the state transition stored?** A. In the state (it calls `m.setState`), which keeps transition knowledge local; a table-driven machine is the alternative for large machines.
- **Q. How would a coin reserve be added?** A. Give `ChangeMaker` a coin inventory, return `Optional<List<Integer>>`, and refund when it is empty.
- **Q. State versus Strategy?** A. State changes by itself as events occur; a strategy is chosen by the client and stays.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
State pattern: one class per status, with default methods rejecting unsupported operations.

- Order every operation as validate, compute, mutate; guarantee a way out of every state.
- Greedy change is correct for canonical denominations only.
- Separate the user interface from the administrator interface.

Reading the output: with capacity 5 and a rate of 2 per second, a burst of 7 admits 5. One second later exactly 2 tokens exist, so 2 of 4 requests pass. After ten idle seconds the bucket is full again (capped at 5, not 20). The sliding window log admits 3 requests, rejects the fourth, rejects a request at 0.6 s because three entries are still inside the window, and at 1.1 s the old entries have expired. In the last line eight threads made 8 000 calls against a capacity of 100 with no refill, and exactly 100 were admitted.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Why compare-and-set works.** Each attempt reads the immutable state, computes the successor, and publishes it only if nobody changed the state in between. A losing thread loops and recomputes. The loop is lock-free: some thread always makes progress, and no thread holds a lock while descheduled.

**Memory.** The map of buckets grows with the number of distinct keys. For public traffic, evict idle buckets: store the last access time and sweep periodically, or use a cache with expiry after access.

**Comparison of the two algorithms.**

rows: Rate limit is approximate over short intervals
Amortised O(1), worst O(N) for cleanup
blocks.caption: Token bucket against sliding window log.

blocks.text:
**Extensions.** Weighted requests (`tryAcquire(key, permits)`), a blocking `acquire` that waits for tokens, per-tier limits looked up from configuration, metrics for rejected calls. Distributed use: keep the state in a shared store and apply the update atomically (a script or compare-and-set), as covered in the Redis material.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Burst at the window boundary

**Scenario.** A fixed-window counter allows 100 requests per minute.

**Symptoms.** A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00; the backend sees 200 requests in two seconds.

**Diagnosis.** Request timestamps cluster around the window boundary.

**Root cause.** The counter resets at the boundary; the limit is not enforced over an arbitrary window.

**Fix.** Use a sliding window or a token bucket whose capacity bounds the burst.

**Prevention.** Choose the algorithm from the burst requirement, not from implementation convenience.

#### Memory growth from one-time keys

**Scenario.** Rate limiting by IP address on a public endpoint.

**Symptoms.** Heap grows steadily; the bucket map holds millions of entries that were used once.

**Diagnosis.** Heap histogram shows `TokenBucket` instances dominating.

**Root cause.** Buckets are never removed.

**Fix.** Evict buckets idle for longer than the time to refill (a full bucket is equivalent to a new one).

**Prevention.** Every per-key map has an eviction rule.

#### Wall-clock time used for refill

**Scenario.** The limiter uses `System.currentTimeMillis`.

**Symptoms.** After an NTP adjustment the clock moves backwards; elapsed time is negative and the bucket is over- or under-filled.

**Diagnosis.** Negative elapsed values in a debug log.

**Root cause.** Wall-clock time is not monotonic.

**Fix.** Use `System.nanoTime` for intervals; guard with `Math.max(0, elapsed)`.

**Prevention.** Wall clock is for timestamps, monotonic time for durations.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. Token bucket versus leaky bucket?** A. A token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity and then limits the average rate; a leaky bucket releases requests at a constant rate and smooths bursts into a queue or rejects them.
- **Q. Why store immutable state in an** `AtomicReference`**?** A. Tokens and timestamp must change together; two separate atomics could be seen inconsistent. One immutable object swapped by compare-and-set is atomic as a unit.
- **Q. How is the limiter made distributed?** A. Keep the state in a shared store and update it with an atomic operation; accept added latency or use local buckets with a share of the global limit and periodic synchronisation, trading accuracy for speed.
- **Q. What does** `tryAcquire` **return when the key is new?** A. A new bucket starts full, so the first requests pass; start empty if the policy requires warm-up.
- **Q. How are tests made deterministic?** A. The clock is injected as a function; tests advance a variable instead of sleeping.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The limiter is an interface; token bucket and sliding window log are interchangeable strategies.

- Refill lazily from elapsed monotonic time; keep tokens and timestamp in one immutable state swapped by compare-and-set.
- Evict idle keys; inject the clock.
- Token bucket bounds bursts by capacity; the log is exact but costs memory.

### Requirements and use cases

A show has a set of seats. A user selects seats and holds them for five minutes while paying. If payment succeeds the seats become booked; if it fails or the time expires the seats become available again. No seat may ever be sold twice. The distributed version of this problem (payments, database transactions, queues for flash sales) appears in the high-level design of a ticket booking system; this chapter designs the in-process core.

Lazy: expired holds are released when the show is next accessed; a scheduler may also sweep (extension).
Many users contend for the same seats in one JVM.

blocks.text:
The two race lines are the key result. Twenty threads released together by a latch tried to take one seat. The naive check-then-act version admitted several winners (6 in one run, 19 in another; the number varies with scheduling, which is typical of a race), while the locked version admitted exactly one.

### Concurrency and extensions

**Why the naive version fails.** `containsKey` and `put` are each atomic, but another thread can run between them; all threads pass the check before any performs the put. The injected one-millisecond sleep widens the window to make the failure reproducible; without it the window is still there and appears under load.

**Lazy expiry under the lock.** `expireStale` runs while the lock is held and calls `release`, which locks again; `ReentrantLock` allows this. The cost is a scan of all holds per call; keep holds in a priority queue ordered by expiry for large shows.

**Extensions.**

- Scheduled sweep: a `ScheduledExecutorService` calls `summary()` or a dedicated `expire()` periodically, so that seat maps shown to users are fresh even without traffic.
- Payment integration: `confirm` is called by the payment callback; it must be idempotent (a repeated callback for the same hold must not fail the booking).
- Seat categories and pricing: a `Seat` entity with a price strategy.
- Multi-instance: move the state to a database with a conditional update; the hold expiry becomes a column.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Double booking under load

**Scenario.** Seat availability is checked in the controller and the booking is saved in the service.

**Symptoms.** At the start of a popular sale two customers hold tickets for the same seat; support receives complaints.

**Diagnosis.** Booking records show two rows for one seat id within milliseconds.

**Root cause.** Check-then-act across two steps with no atomicity.

**Fix.** One atomic operation: lock in memory, or a conditional update in the database (`UPDATE ... WHERE status =` `'AVAILABLE'` with a check of the affected row count).

**Prevention.** A concurrency test that fires many parallel requests at one seat and asserts one winner; a unique constraint on (show, seat) as a safety net.

#### Seats stuck in HELD

**Scenario.** Users abandon the payment page.

**Symptoms.** The show appears sold out while many seats are held; revenue drops.

**Diagnosis.** Count of HELD seats with `expiresAt` in the past is large.

**Root cause.** Release depends on the user completing or cancelling; there was no expiry.

**Fix.** Hold with expiry, enforced lazily and by a periodic sweep.

**Prevention.** Every temporary reservation has a deadline.

#### Late payment confirmation for an expired hold

**Scenario.** The payment succeeds at minute 5:10 and the confirmation arrives after the hold expired and another user took the seat.

**Symptoms.** The customer is charged without a ticket.

**Diagnosis.** `HoldExpiredException` on confirm, with a successful payment record.

**Root cause.** Payment time is not bounded by the hold time.

**Fix.** Refund automatically on `HoldExpiredException`; extend the hold when the payment starts; give the payment a timeout shorter than the hold.

**Prevention.** Treat confirm failure after payment as a compensating action in the saga.

### Questions to expect

- **Q. How is overselling prevented across several servers?** A. The atomic claim moves to the shared store: a conditional update or a transaction with a unique constraint; an in-memory lock does not span processes.
- **Q. Why all-or-nothing for multi-seat holds?** A. A partial hold would leave the user with some seats and a failed request; validating all seats before changing any gives a clean rejection.
- **Q. Why is deadlock impossible here?** A. There is one lock per show and no operation holds two show locks. With per-seat locks, deadlock is avoided by acquiring in sorted order.
- **Q. How are expired holds released if nobody calls the show?** A. A scheduled task sweeps periodically; lazy expiry guarantees correctness, the sweep guarantees freshness.
- **Q. What if the confirm callback is delivered twice?** A. The second call finds no hold; return success if the seats are already booked for that hold id, so the callback is idempotent.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The core is one atomic transition per operation under a lock per show: hold validates all seats, then marks them.

- Never check and act in separate steps; demonstrate the race with a test.
- Holds have a deadline, enforced lazily and by a sweep; confirm after expiry fails and triggers a refund.
- Across servers the atomic step becomes a conditional database update.
